content: Acetylsalicylic acid, commonly known as aspirin, is a medication used for various medical purposes. Prescription aspirin is primarily utilized to alleviate symptoms associated with rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and other rheumatologic conditions. Rheumatoid arthritis involves joint inflammation, while osteoarthritis results from the breakdown of joint linings. Systemic lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks joints and organs, causing pain and swelling. Nonprescription aspirin is commonly used to reduce fever and relieve mild to moderate pain, such as headaches, menstrual cramps, arthritis pain, colds, toothaches, and muscle aches. Additionally, it is used to prevent heart attacks in individuals with a history of heart attacks or angina (chest pain due to insufficient oxygen supply to the heart). It also reduces the risk of death in people experiencing or who have recently experienced a heart attack. Furthermore, aspirin is used to prevent ischemic strokes (caused by blood clots blocking blood flow to the brain) or transient ischemic attacks (mini-strokes) in individuals with a history of such events. However, aspirin does not prevent hemorrhagic strokes (caused by bleeding in the brain). Aspirin belongs to a class of medications called salicylates. It works by inhibiting the production of certain natural substances in the body that cause fever, pain, swelling, and blood clots. Aspirin is also available in combination with other medications, such as antacids, pain relievers, and cough and cold medications. This information pertains specifically to aspirin as a standalone medication. If you are using a combination product, consult the package or prescription label or ask your doctor or pharmacist for more details. Prescription aspirin is available as an extended-release tablet, which releases the medication slowly over time. Nonprescription aspirin comes in various forms, including regular tablets, enteric-coated delayed-release tablets, chewable tablets, gum, and rectal suppositories. Prescription aspirin is typically taken two or more times daily, while nonprescription aspirin is often taken once daily to lower the risk of heart attack or stroke. For fever or pain relief, nonprescription aspirin is usually taken every 4–6 hours as needed. Follow the instructions on the package or prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take aspirin exactly as directed, without exceeding or reducing the recommended dose. Swallow extended-release tablets whole with a full glass of water; do not break, crush, or chew them. Regular tablets should also be swallowed with a full glass of water. Chewable aspirin tablets can be chewed, crushed, or swallowed whole, followed by a full glass of water. Consult a doctor before giving aspirin to children or teenagers, as it may cause Reye's syndrome, a serious condition involving fat accumulation in the brain, liver, and other organs, especially if they have a viral illness like chickenpox or the flu. If you have had oral surgery or tonsil removal within the past seven days, consult your doctor about which types of aspirin are safe for you. Delayed-release tablets take time to start working and should not be used for fever or pain requiring immediate relief. Discontinue aspirin and contact your doctor if your fever persists for more than three days, your pain lasts longer than ten days, or the affected area becomes red or swollen. These symptoms may indicate a condition requiring medical attention. To use an aspirin suppository rectally, remove the wrapper, moisten the tip with water, and insert it into the rectum. For infants and children, insert about ½ to 1 inch; for adults, insert about 1 inch. Hold it in place for a few moments and avoid standing for at least 15 minutes. Wash your hands thoroughly afterward. Aspirin is also sometimes used to treat rheumatic fever, a serious condition that may develop after a strep throat infection and cause heart valve swelling, and Kawasaki disease, an illness that can lead to heart problems in children. Additionally, it may be used to reduce the risk of blood clots in patients with artificial heart valves or certain heart conditions and to prevent certain pregnancy complications. Before taking aspirin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to aspirin, other pain or fever medications, tartrazine dye, or any other substances. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. Mention specific medications such as acetazolamide, ACE inhibitors, anticoagulants, beta blockers, diuretics, diabetes or arthritis medications, gout medications, methotrexate, NSAIDs, phenytoin, and valproic acid. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. If you are taking aspirin regularly to prevent heart attack or stroke, consult your doctor before using ibuprofen for pain or fever, as it may interfere with aspirin's effectiveness. Allow sufficient time between taking your daily aspirin dose and ibuprofen. Inform your doctor if you have asthma, frequent nasal congestion, nasal polyps, heartburn, stomach pain, ulcers, anemia, bleeding disorders, or kidney or liver disease. Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals should consult their doctor before taking aspirin, as it may harm the fetus or cause delivery complications if taken during the last months of pregnancy. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking aspirin. If you consume three or more alcoholic drinks daily, consult your doctor about the safety of taking aspirin or other pain and fever medications. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking aspirin. If you miss a dose of regularly scheduled aspirin, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Aspirin may cause side effects. Common minor side effects include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, and heartburn. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects include hives, rash, swelling of the eyes, face, lips, tongue, or throat, wheezing, difficulty breathing, hoarseness, rapid heartbeat, cold and clammy skin, ringing in the ears, hearing loss, bloody vomit, vomit resembling coffee grounds, bright red blood in stools, or black or tarry stools. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Report serious side effects to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store aspirin in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture. Store suppositories in a cool place or refrigerator. Discard expired or unused medication and tablets with a strong vinegar smell. Consult your pharmacist for proper disposal methods. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual has collapsed or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose include burning pain in the throat or stomach, vomiting, decreased urination, fever, restlessness, irritability, confusion, hallucinations, seizures, drowsiness, or loss of consciousness. Keep all medical appointments and do not share your prescription aspirin with others. Consult your pharmacist for any questions about refilling your prescription.
